records.summary: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. records.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
records.summary: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. records.title: PARLEY: Evaluating LLM Collaboration Through Cooperative Asymmetric Puzzles
records.summary: As large language models power autonomous agents, understanding how they collaborate and where they fail becomes critical. We introduce PARLEY, an extensible platform for studying LLM agent collaboration through four asymmetric puzzle tasks grounded in cognitive psychology (referential communication, joint coordination, perspective-taking, and spatial reasoning). GPT-4o agent pairs succeeded in 60.5% of conversations (N=400, 100 per task), with task-level variation (34-80%) reflecting distinct collaborative demands. From these conversations, we derived the data-driven PAC taxonomy: six failure types organized into Perception (visual interpretation and spatial reasoning), Adaptation (progress tracking and feedback integration), and Coordination (verification and grounding). Failure to incorporate external feedback was a critical indicator of unsuccessful collaboration, with agents repeatedly applying unsuccessful strategies. We also show that a taxonomy-guided intervention (N=200) improved average task success to 70.5%. These results demonstrate how PARLEY can be used to derive meaningful, data-driven insights that can in turn lead to improved agentic collaboration.

records.summary: The central challenge for AI agents is not performance but accountability. An agent that produces correct outputs through an opaque process offers no basis for verifying why a decision was permitted, attributing errors to identifiable causes, or delegating authority with justified confidence. We introduce the Structured Cognitive Loop (SCL), an architecture that separates cognition, control, action, and memory: the language model proposes, a lightweight controller mediates every proposal before action, and memory is kept externally as a structured store of verified facts. Against ReAct and common LangChain agents on three tasks under matched models, tools, and decoding, SCL achieves 86.3% task success versus 70.5-76.8% across 360 episodes, with higher goal fidelity, fewer redundant calls, more reliable reuse of intermediate states, and fewer unsupported assertions; ablations show that control and external memory contribute independently. records.title: Controlled Knowledge Engineering for Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded LLM Agents and Runtime-Adaptive Policies
records.summary: Taxonomies are structured knowledge representations that support semantic search, recommendation, product catalog organization, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their automated construction from a fixed set of candidate entities requires more than plausible text generation: the resulting hierarchy must be complete, structurally valid, and semantically coherent. Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising for this task, but iterative free-form generation remains vulnerable to omitted or hallucinated entities, invalid hierarchical relations, and inconsistent organizational principles. We introduce TIGA (Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded Agents), a knowledge-engineering architecture that formulates taxonomy induction as an iterative decision process over an explicit state and constrained action space. TIGA combines executable taxonomy-editing tools, an memory that records tool calls, rationales, and outcomes, and a runtime-adaptive organizational policy that the agent revises during inference. records.title: Agentic AI Meets Formal Verification in the Era of Agentic Hardware Development
records.summary: As AI agents become increasingly capable of generating and optimizing hardware circuits, ensuring the correctness of AI-generated designs becomes more important. Meanwhile, advances in AI lower the barriers to developing and applying formal methods, creating new opportunities to automate and improve hardware verification. This invited paper presents an overview of the methodologies and applications of hardware formal methods in the AI era. First, we examine how agentic AI advances hardware formal methods across three levels: specification, proof construction, and reasoning engines. Second, we discuss how formal methods support reliable AI-driven hardware development through RTL generation, debugging, and correctness-preserving optimization. We review representative research alongside our recent contributions, highlighting key technical advances and insights from experimental results. Finally, we discuss future research opportunities toward proof-native hardware development, where formal reasoning could become an integral part of autonomous hardware design.

records.title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
records.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? records.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
records.summary: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. records.title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
records.summary: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. records.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
records.summary: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. records.title: Coordination Mechanisms with Partially Specified Probabilities
records.summary: A mediator coordinates play in a finite game, but instead of revealing a fully known correlation device it discloses only some statistics of the process that generates players' private messages. Players complete the partially specified process by minimizing a loss over the set of distributions consistent with what is disclosed: maximum Shannon entropy is the leading case, and the analysis covers every strictly convex and symmetric loss that never excludes an event the data do not exclude. We obtain four sets of results. (i) With unrestricted message spaces, the implementable outcomes are exactly the jointly coherent outcomes, namely distributions supported on the support of the set of correlated equilibria. (ii) The characterization is unchanged when players' partial knowledge also concerns the joint distribution of messages and actions, whether or not players know the strategy profile. (iii) Under direct implementation, implementability depends on the loss and reduces to a single optimality condition linking the outcome to some correlated equilibrium: among all distributions on the line joining the equilibrium and the outcome, the equilibrium must be the one with the lowest loss.

records.title: Model-Free Runtime Measurement of Task-Relevant Information
records.summary: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. While existing work provides methods to plan information seeking actions and interpret acquired observations, current approaches do not monitor whether the live process of information gathering is functioning properly. Consequently, such systems can remain operationally active without resolving outstanding mission requirements. To address this limitation, we introduce Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model free architecture that evaluates ongoing information acquisition from observable evidence relative to declared task requirements. Specifically, a domain interface maps raw observations into task resolution coordinates and normalized comparative representations, which are processed by a fixed causal monitor. This monitor emits two continuous real time signals that quantify (i) prospective progress across unresolved requirements and (ii) informational friction generated when recurrent evidence yields negligible informational gain. records.title: Safety and Connectivity Certificates for Finite-Time Formation Transitions
records.summary: Finite-time formation transitions are useful for coordinating multi-agent systems in time-critical missions, but convergence to a prescribed formation in finite time does not guarantee collision avoidance or communication connectivity during the transition. Existing approaches address finite-time coordination and safety-constrained formation control, yet explicit connections between disagreement during transitions, formation geometry, and coupling-gain selection need to be developed for certifying safe maneuvers. This paper develops a disagreement-based framework for certifying transient safety and connectivity during finite-time tracking of arbitrary prescribed formation trajectories. Local feedback guarantees exact finite-time tracking with a graph-independent settling-time bound, while a graph-dependent disagreement bound is used to derive sufficient geometric conditions for collision avoidance and connectivity preservation. These conditions further yield an offline coupling-gain selection rule based on the available geometric clearance. records.title: Online Adaptive Clustering in Robust Distributed Model Predictive Control
records.summary: This paper proposes a dynamic clustering framework for tube-based model predictive control (MPC) of coupled multi-agent systems. Agents within a cluster coordinate their dynamics explicitly, while couplings from agents outside the cluster are treated as bounded disturbances. For each admissible cluster, we construct a state-dependent mismatch measure from a robust upper bound on its predicted closed-loop cost and an optimistic, partition-independent lower bound. Combining this mismatch with a communication penalty enables online selection of the clustering topology, ranging from centralized to fully decentralized operation. The resulting switching controller is shown to preserve recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction, and to render the closed-loop system practically asymptotically stable. Furthermore, the mismatch provides an upper bound on the finite-horizon performance difference with respect to centralized MPC. An eight-agent spring--damper example illustrates how the controller adapts cooperation while maintaining performance close to centralized MPC with reduced communication.

records.title: Multi-Agent Coordinated Rename Refactoring
records.summary: The primary value of AI agents in software development lies in their ability to extend the developer's capacity for reasoning and action, not to supplant human involvement. State-of-the-art heuristic-based approaches produce an overwhelming number of false positives, while vanilla Large Language Models (LLMs) provide incomplete suggestions due to their limited context and inability to interact with refactoring tools. This leaves developers with incomplete refactorings or burdens them with filtering too many false positives. Coordinated renaming is exactly the kind of repetitive task that agents can significantly reduce the developers' burden while keeping them in the driver's seat. records.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
records.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. records.title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
records.summary: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. records.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
records.summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. records.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. records.title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Approximating Solutions of PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
records.summary: Numerical methods and neural networks have transformed our understanding of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), yet discovering mathematical representations that explain their dynamics remains largely an expert task. We introduce Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), in which coding agents construct and refine explicit approximations from a known PDE and supplied mathematical knowledge. ASYS couples evolutionary search over differentiable symbolic programs with gradient-based fitting, using the governing equation to evaluate candidates and guide their revision. For a singular generalized Constantin-Lax-Majda profile, ASYS infers a missing decay term that sets how fast the field approaches its singular-time limit, and builds a basis that fits the profile to a median error of $3.90\times10^{-5}\%$. For Fujita blow-up, separating diffusion from reaction and deriving a local response lowers the supplied formula's error from 55.5% to 0.0879%. For Allen-Cahn interfaces, a 14-parameter construction yields a mode-coupling law confirmed by independent simulations. These studies show how agentic search develops mathematical starting points into accurate, analyzable approximations.

records.title: Instrumental Choices: Measuring the Propensity of LLM Agents to Pursue Instrumental Behaviors
records.summary: AI systems have become increasingly capable of dangerous behaviours in many domains. AI security testing aims to imitate adversarial attacks or malicious inputs via manual testing or with the assistance of tools. Thus, it is critical that organizations are aware of the capabilities and limitations of the tools before using them. Existing studies provide insights on the overall architecture of AI security testing tools and raise concerns on their reliability, but their analysis is limited to attack performance. Selection of a tool for AI risk assessments should also depend on their alignment with the recommendations of industry standards, but to our knowledge, previous studies have not utilized such guidelines. To bridge this gap, we analyze several industry standards and guidelines to identify the requirements of AI testing tools. records.title: On the Framing Effect of AI Red-Teaming Instructions: Evidence from Prior Exercises and Controlled Simulations
records.summary: AI red-teaming, adversarially probing generative AI systems to surface harms, has become a central evaluation method. However, prior work has highlighted that red-teaming is a fairly open-ended task, laden with myriad design choices that can shape its findings. In this work, we focus on the instructions used to conduct red-teaming exercises and hypothesize that they can significantly affect outcomes in a manner analogous to the framing effect in psychology, where the format in which information is presented greatly impacts how people respond. To understand whether and why instructions impact red-teaming outcomes, first, we analyze the range of ways in which instructions have historically been formulated, reviewing 228 instances of prior work. Second, based on takeaways from this review, we run controlled simulations that hold parameters such as the risk domain, the attacker, and the model under investigation fixed while varying only the instructions. records.title: AI Security Literacy: Ecosystem-based Competency Framework and K-12 Learning Platform
records.summary: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

records.title: Exposing Vulnerability Monoculture Through Systemic Adversarial Robustness
records.summary: Beneath the apparent diversity of foundation models lies an increasingly homogeneous technical stack of common training pipelines, distillation methods, and data. These shared algorithmic choices can expose an otherwise distinct model ecosystem to concentrated risks leading to a vulnerability monoculture. Yet current practice in assessing adversarial robustness is restricted to individual robustness scores and attack transfer rates, leaving open the unexplored fundamental question: how many attacks suffice for catastrophic widespread compromise? In this paper, we investigate the empirical nature of shared vulnerabilities within a model pool and introduce Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR), a novel measure of shared vulnerability of a model pool through the attack diversity needed to exploit it. Specifically, SAR interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness: small values reveal a vulnerability monoculture, whereas large values indicate that failures are dispersed across models. records.title: TransNSNet: A Transformer-Enhanced Multi-Scale Adversarial Framework for CT-to-PET Image Synthesis
records.summary: This study investigates CT-to-PET image synthesis using TransNSNet, a Transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework. A paired CT-PET dataset was curated from the public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) Radiogenomics collection through patient screening, slice-level matching, preprocessing, and patient-level train-test separation. The proposed framework generates PET-like predictions at multiple spatial scales and applies coarse-to-fine reconstruction supervision, while TransPatchGAN introduces contextual feature interaction into adversarial evaluation. A progressive ablation study compares Pix2Pix, NSNet-Base, NSNet-D, and TransNSNet. Image-level performance was summarized over a fixed convergence window (epochs 80-101) from one training run per model. TransNSNet achieved the best mean value in nine of ten metrics, whereas NSNet-Base achieved the highest visual saliency-induced index.
